opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. It's a great question, and the honest answer is: partly, and in a way that surprised a lot of us.

When the early AI people started out decades ago, they borrowed a very crude cartoon of the brain. A neuron gets inputs, adds them up, and if they pass a threshold it fires. That was the "artificial neuron." Neuroscientists like me looked at it and said, this is a toy; a real neuron is enormously more complicated, with chemistry, timing, and dendrites doing their own computation. And we were right about that.

What's interesting is that once you stack billions of these toy units and train them on enormous amounts of data, some of the behaviour that comes out looks eerily familiar. In my lab and others we've compared what happens inside these networks to what happens inside a human brain when you show it the same picture or the same sentence, and you find similar layers of representation. Early on you get edges and simple features, later you get faces, objects, concepts. Language models also do something the brain does all the time: they predict what comes next. A lot of what your brain is doing right now, listening to me, is guessing my next word and only paying attention when I surprise it.

So in that sense, yes, they stumbled onto some of the same solutions, probably because those solutions are just good ways of dealing with the world.

But I'd be careful about saying they replicated the brain. A child learns what a dog is from a handful of examples; these models need millions. Your brain runs on about twenty watts, roughly a dim light bulb, while these systems need data centres. And the brain isn't just a prediction machine sitting in a jar. It's in a body, it's driven by hunger, fear, love, wanting to stay alive. Emotion isn't a bug in human decision-making; it's how we decide what matters. The models don't have that, at least not yet.

The way I like to put it: AI didn't copy the brain, it rediscovered a few of the brain's tricks. And that's actually useful for people like me, because we can now poke inside a system that behaves a bit like a mind in ways we could never ethically poke inside a person. So in a funny way, the machines we built to imitate us are starting to teach us about ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says language models predict what comes next, but does not explain how language lets humans coordinate around abstract ideas.

r002.rationale: The response does not frame giving AI language as transferring a capacity that gave humans an evolutionary advantage over other species.

fable-5.1.text:
Accidentally? No. But I think they've stumbled into something that rhymes with the brain, and that's more interesting than if they'd copied it on purpose.

Let me explain what I mean. When I started in neuroscience, the idea that you'd take a very simple unit, a neuron, connect billions of them, and get something like thought out of it, that was a story we told ourselves. We didn't have a way to test it. And then a bunch of engineers who were not trying to understand the brain, who honestly didn't care much about the brain, built a thing out of very simple units, connected a huge number of them, fed them a lot of data, and out came something that writes poetry and passes the bar exam. So in one sense, they ran the experiment we couldn't run, and the result came back saying, yes, this basic architecture is enough to get a lot of what we thought was special.

But here's where I push back on the word "replicated." The brain is not a text predictor. The brain is a body-regulation machine that got hijacked for language late in the game. It runs on about twenty watts, it learns from a handful of examples, it has a reward system wired to hunger and fear and sex and status, and it sleeps, which turns out to matter enormously for how memory consolidates. None of that is in these models. So when people say "it's a brain," I say, it's a brain the way an airplane is a bird. We learned something real about flight from birds. The airplane flies. But it doesn't lay eggs, and you shouldn't expect it to.

What keeps me up at night is the other direction. We're now using these models to study the brain, because they're the first thing we can open up and look at all the parameters. And some of the structures we find inside them, the way they represent concepts in geometry, look suspiciously like what we see when we record from human neurons. So the honest answer is: they didn't replicate the brain. They built a mirror, and we're just starting to figure out which parts of the reflection are us.

r001.rationale: The response says language was a late use of the brain and mentions models writing, but does not explain how language lets humans coordinate around abstract ideas.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between replicating the brain and discovering some of the same principles. We haven’t built a human brain. But we’ve built systems that learn from examples, adjust connections, and develop internal representations that we didn’t explicitly design. There’s a resemblance there.

The interesting question is whether that resemblance comes from borrowing ideas from neuroscience, or whether any system trying to solve similar problems ends up finding similar solutions. You and a machine both need to recognize a face under different lighting, for instance. There may be useful ways of solving that problem that both systems discover.

But similar behavior doesn’t necessarily mean the same mechanism. And it certainly doesn’t establish that the machine has a subjective experience. So I’d say we may have rediscovered pieces of how brains process information. Replicated the human brain? That’s a much stronger claim.

r001.rationale: The response discusses similarities between machine learning and brain processes, but does not explain how language lets humans coordinate around abstract ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “accidentally” is doing a lot of work there. We borrowed an idea from the brain—that you can have many simple units connected together, and that changing the connections allows you to learn. But that doesn’t mean we’ve replicated the brain.

What’s interesting is that, when you train these systems to solve problems we solve, you sometimes see similar patterns emerge. And then the question is: did they discover something about how the brain works, or is that just a useful solution that very different systems can arrive at?

So I would say we’ve built something that resembles certain aspects of human cognition. Whether it gets there the same way we do is a much harder question.
